Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Combat Pilot
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Stop Enjoyment: give up pleasant activities, Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Dmitri Voss is a 56-year-old married combat pilot who has spent the better part of three decades flying fighter aircraft, a career built on precision, composure, and an almost constitutional belief that skill and discipline could hold catastrophe at bay. That belief was dismantled in a single afternoon eighteen months ago, when a catastrophic hydraulic failure during a training sortie sent his aircraft into an uncontrolled descent at low altitude. The sequence unfolded with a speed that outpaced any procedural response: a sudden violent shudder through the airframe, warning tones stacking on top of one another in the cockpit, and then an explosion from somewhere aft of the fuselage — a percussive concussive blast that he felt in his chest and teeth before he consciously registered hearing it. The ejection seat fired. What followed was a period of violent disorientation — spinning, pressure, the world tilting without reference — before he lost consciousness briefly and came to on the ground with a fractured vertebra, a ruptured eardrum, and the aircraft burning in a field three hundred metres away.

In the weeks after the accident, Dmitri returned to his family home and attempted to resume something resembling his former life. He told his wife he was fine. He believed, for a time, that he meant it. But the body kept a different account. He noticed that unexpected movement at the periphery of his vision — a technician stepping quickly around a corner, his wife reaching suddenly across the table — produced an immediate and involuntary physical response: muscles bracing, breath catching, hands moving before thought could intervene. He found himself scanning rooms when he entered them, tracking exits, noting what was overhead and what might fall. He had come to believe, in a way he could not fully articulate, that the world had revealed itself to be structurally unreliable — that the orderly, skill-governed universe he had inhabited as a pilot no longer existed, and that something dangerous could emerge from any ordinary moment without warning.

The triggers that reached him most reliably were physical ones. A sudden bang — a car backfiring on the base road, a door slamming in the officers' mess — could stop him mid-stride. More disturbing to him was what happened in his own body: episodes of dizziness or lightheadedness, which arose unpredictably, would flood him with a sensory recognition he could not suppress. The spinning, the loss of horizon, the feeling of a world that would not hold still — these sensations carried him back to the ejection with an immediacy that bore no relationship to ordinary memory. On days when he felt physically unwell for any reason, the effect was similar: a diffuse, nauseating sense that something was already going wrong, that the body could not be trusted.

He had, over the months, quietly reorganised his life around these vulnerabilities. He declined a mandatory flight medical, citing a scheduling conflict he never resolved, and had not set foot in the base medical centre since his discharge from hospital. He had stopped attending the informal social evenings he and his wife had shared with other pilot families for years, and had withdrawn from a weekly hiking group he had joined before the accident. What frightened him most about these activities was not their content but their unpredictability — the sense that enjoyment required a kind of openness to experience that now felt dangerous. He had also begun controlling his food intake with an unusual rigidity, eating the same small meals at the same times each day. He could not fully explain this to himself, but the discipline of it — the one domain in which outcomes remained exactly as anticipated — offered something that felt necessary.

His wife noticed the changes before he acknowledged them. She described a man who was physically present but somehow absent, and her word — "hollow" — lodged in him because it matched something he already knew. He felt dead inside in a way that no amount of effort seemed to reach. It was she who finally suggested he speak to someone, and it was the prospect of losing her trust, more than any symptom, that brought him to the intake appointment. What he most fears, sitting across from the clinician now, is that nothing of who he was before that afternoon can be recovered. What he most hopes, though he has not yet said it aloud, is to be proved wrong.
